caption:
Sam Altman was asked on Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast why Mira Murati, Ilya Sutskever, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk went their own way.
His answer: when the stakes feel this high, many people "only trust themselves to build this."
He also named the two ways he thinks AI could go badly wrong.

Do you think he is right about why they left?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Figuring Out with Raj Shamani, Android Headlines · Photo: reuters.com
threads_text: Sam Altman's explanation for why so many OpenAI leaders left to build rival AI: when the stakes feel this high, people "only trust themselves to build this." It is also a neat way of saying the problem was never him. Do you buy that answer?

site_article.headline: Sam Altman says departing OpenAI leaders 'only trust themselves to build this'
site_article.dek: On the Figuring Out podcast, the OpenAI chief executive linked the exits of former colleagues to fears about who should hold power over advanced AI.
site_article.summary: Sam Altman told podcast host Raj Shamani that many people who left OpenAI to start or lead rival AI efforts came to trust only themselves with the technology. He also described two ways he believes AI could go badly wrong.
site_article.seo_title: Sam Altman on why OpenAI leaders left to build rival AI
site_article.seo_description: On Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, Sam Altman said people who left OpenAI often only trust themselves to build AI, and named his two biggest AI risks.
site_article.answer_summary: Altman said that when the stakes feel high, many people only trust themselves to build advanced AI, and a disagreement about approach turns into a refusal to let power concentrate in someone else's hands.

paragraphs.text: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman offered his explanation for why several of the company's best known leaders left to build competing AI efforts, in an interview on the Figuring Out podcast hosted by Raj Shamani. A transcript of the episode was published on November 3, 2026.

Shamani raised the departures and rival projects involving former chief technology officer Mira Murati, co-founder Ilya Sutskever, former research leader Dario Amodei and co-founder Elon Musk. Each of the four left OpenAI and went on to establish or lead a competing AI venture, according to coverage of the interview.

Altman did not name any individual in his answer. He said that something happens in many people's minds when the stakes feel this high, so that they only trust themselves to build the technology. In his telling, a disagreement over technical approach becomes a question of power: a person concludes that a rival's approach is bad and that power therefore cannot be allowed to concentrate in that rival's hands.

Elsewhere in the conversation, Altman said he personally dislikes intense concentration of power. Android Headlines noted that his comments came alongside a broader argument that several competing labs, each pursuing different technical approaches, make the world safer than a single gatekeeper would.
Two ways AI could go wrong

Asked about his biggest worries, Altman described two failure modes. The first is a loss of control to AI, in which people intentionally or accidentally hand over control of the future to the systems they build. The second is that one person, company or country becomes far too powerful relative to everyone else. Android Headlines described the pair as the ways Altman thinks the technology could go cartoonishly wrong.

Altman said he believes in pluralism and favors multiple competing AI efforts over a single dominant one. He also said he expects OpenAI's work to be a net positive for the world despite the responsibility it carries.
What Altman sees as OpenAI's edge

When Shamani asked about OpenAI's competitive advantages, Altman pointed to the company having the most users and a full stack that runs from chips to data centers to models, along with its brand and values. Speaking about himself, he cited the length of time he has spent in the field and his connections across the industry, while acknowledging that Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis has been working on AI for longer.

Shamani also asked why roughly 700 employees threatened to resign when Altman was fired. Altman credited a mission driven team and a culture that combines strong conviction with open mindedness, rather than his own role alone. He also said he is extremely excited to see how far AI can be pushed to discover new science.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the answer is notable for what it leaves out. Altman frames the exits as a general pattern of distrust among people who feel the stakes are enormous, rather than as a response to specific decisions at OpenAI. That framing also fits his larger argument that many competing labs are healthier than one, since each departure added another rival to the field.
Altman's account is one side of these splits. Watch whether any of the four people raised in the interview respond to his description of why they left OpenAI.
